topic.examWeightHint: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. A trigonometric graph has opened an early question in every paper read: Summer 2018 Q3(a) (sine, 2 marks), Summer 2019 Q4(a) (cosine, 2), Summer 2022 Q4(a) (sine over a negative range, 1), Summer 2023 Q3(a) (cosine from -180 to 180, 2) and Summer 2025 Q2(a) (tangent, 1). The axes are printed for you and the wording is either Sketch the graph of or Complete the graph of, with the range written underneath. The marks are for the shape and for the scale or key points, one each. The part that follows almost always solves an equation on the same curve for 2 or 3 marks, and the readings are marked against the candidate's own graph, so an accurate sketch is paid for twice.

Radians: every angle in Unit 1 is measured in degrees

Amplitude as a variable quantity: with no stretches on this specification it is always 1

A trigonometric graph has opened an early question in every paper read: Summer 2018 Q3(a) (sine, 2 marks), Summer 2019 Q4(a) (cosine, 2), Summer 2022 Q4(a) (sine over a negative range, 1), Summer 2023 Q3(a) (cosine from -180 to 180, 2) and Summer 2025 Q2(a) (tangent, 1). The axes are printed for you and the wording is either Sketch the graph of or Complete the graph of, with the range written underneath. The marks are for the shape and for the scale or key points, one each. The part that follows almost always solves an equation on the same curve for 2 or 3 marks, and the readings are marked against the candidate's own graph, so an accurate sketch is paid for twice.
traps: Joining the key points with straight lines instead of one smooth curve, which earns the points and loses the shape (Summer 2018 FM1 Q3, Summer 2019 FM1 Q4)
Leaving the axes without a scale, so the values mean nothing (Summer 2022 FM1 Q4, Summer 2023 FM1 Q3)
Starting a cosine sketch at the origin, which is the sine curve drawn by mistake (Summer 2022 FM1 Q4)
Leaving the asymptotes off a tangent sketch, or drawing them at 180° (Summer 2025 FM1 Q2)
Letting the tangent curve touch or cross an asymptote (Summer 2025 FM1 Q2)
Running off the bottom of the grid instead of turning at the minimum (Summer 2023 FM1 Q3)
Giving 360° as the period of tan x, or 180° as the period of sin x
Changing the sign when using symmetry, which reflects the curve in the x-axis instead of sideways
Stopping at the calculator's angle when the drawn line clearly cuts the curve twice (Summer 2022 FM1 Q4)

steps.decision: Plot before you draw. The five points fix the whole curve, and they are also what the scheme credits when the curve itself is not smooth enough.

steps.working: Join them with one smooth curve and mark $90$, $180$, $270$, $360$ along the x-axis and $1$ and $-1$ up the y-axis.
steps.decision: The scale is a mark of its own, and it costs four numbers and two more. Straight sides between the turning points throw away the shape mark.

options: Because the curve has to be smooth and the axes have to carry a scale
Because the curve is made of straight lines
Because the y-axis runs from 0 to 360
whyMenu.explain: Shape and scale are the two things a sketch mark is for. Everything else on the page is decoration.

steps.working: Draw the line $y = 0.6$ across the graph. It cuts the curve $2$ times.
steps.decision: Counting the crossings first tells you how many answers to look for, so you cannot stop at one by mistake.
The calculator always gives the angle in the first quadrant here, and that is the one the picture shows on the way up.
The arch is symmetrical about $x = 90^\circ$, so the second angle is as far past the mirror as the first is short of it. Reading it off the graph gives about $140^\circ$, which agrees.

steps.decision: $\tan x$ is the up measurement divided by the across one, and across is zero at those two angles, so there is no value of the function there at all.

options: Because $\cos x$ is zero there, so the division has no answer
Because the curve has a maximum there
Because the angle is too large
whyMenu.explain: An asymptote marks a missing value, not a turning point. That is why the curve can run off in both directions beside it.

steps.decision: These are the anchors between the asymptotes. Mark them before drawing anything curved.

steps.working: In the strip $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ the curve rises from the origin and climbs steeply towards the dashed line without meeting it.
steps.decision: Steeply towards, never onto. A sketch whose curve touches an asymptote is marked as a misunderstanding of what an asymptote is.

steps.working: Each of the next two strips holds the same branch again, because the pattern repeats every $180^\circ$.
steps.decision: Copy, do not invent. One branch drawn well and repeated twice is a complete answer, and the period is the fact that licenses the copying.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Three identical branches, with dashed asymptotes at $x = 90$ and $x = 270$ and crossings at $0^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $360^\circ$

items.stem:
Three quick checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new work, so answer from what you already know.
In a right-angled triangle, which ratio is $\sin \theta$?

options.feedback: That is the one. It is also why the sine curve never leaves the strip between -1 and 1: the opposite side can never be longer than the hypotenuse.
That is cosine. The two are easy to swap, and swapping them is what makes a sketch start in the wrong place.
That is tangent, which has no hypotenuse in it at all and so is not trapped between -1 and 1.

items.stem: A curve passes through the point where $x = 4$ and $y = -3$. How are those coordinates written?

options.feedback: Across first, then up or down. Every coordinate answer in this topic is written the same way.
The two numbers are right and they are the wrong way round. The x-value always comes first.
The order here is right. Brackets are how a pair is written, and a mark scheme asking for coordinates expects them.

items.stem: On a calculator set to degrees, what is $\sin 30^\circ$?
items.skill: Prerequisite: reading a trigonometric value in degrees

options.feedback: Good. If your calculator gives something else, it is in radians, and every answer in Unit 1 would then come out wrong.
The angle goes in and a ratio comes out. That ratio is always between -1 and 1 for sine.
That is $\sin 30$ in radians. Set the calculator to degrees before you start.

items.stem: Which curve passes through the point $(0, 1)$?
items.skill: Tell the sine and cosine curves apart

options.feedback: Cosine starts at its maximum, so it is at 1 when the angle is zero.
$\sin 0^\circ = 0$, so the sine curve starts at the origin and climbs from there.
$\tan 0^\circ = 0$ as well, so the tangent curve also starts on the axis.

items.stem: What is the period of $y = \tan x$?
items.skill: Recall the period of each curve

options.feedback: Half the period of the other two. One branch, then the same branch again.
$360^\circ$ is the period of sine and cosine. The tangent curve has already repeated once by then.
$90^\circ$ is the gap from a crossing to an asymptote, which is half a branch rather than a whole one.

items.stem: Where are the asymptotes of $y = \tan x$ in the range $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$?
items.skill: Place the asymptotes of the tangent curve

options.feedback: Those are the angles where the across measurement is zero, so the division that makes tan has no answer.
Those are the angles where the curve crosses the axis, which is the opposite of a break.
Both of those are crossings as well. The breaks sit halfway between them.

items.stem: A sketch of $y = \sin x$ has all five key points plotted correctly, joined by straight lines. How is it marked?
items.skill: Know what the shape mark is for

options.text: The points earn their mark; the shape mark is lost
options.feedback: Examiners have said this for several series running. Joining the points in one smooth pass is the whole difference.

options.text: Full marks, because the points are right
options.feedback: The shape is a separate mark, and straight sides between the turning points are what it is checking for.
Positive marking credits the right values. Only the shape mark goes.

items.skill: Use the symmetry of the sine curve

options.feedback: $180 - 50 = 130$, and the arch is symmetrical about $x = 90^\circ$, so the height is unchanged.
Changing the sign reflects the curve in the x-axis. The symmetry here is sideways, and it leaves the height where it was.
That is $\cos 50^\circ$. The question stays on the sine curve throughout.

items.stem: The sine curve is drawn for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$ and a horizontal line is drawn at $y = 0.4$. How many solutions does that give?
items.skill: Count the solutions a range holds

options.feedback: The line cuts the arch twice, once going up and once coming down, and the rest of the curve stays below it.
The calculator gives one angle. The picture shows the curve reaching that height a second time before the range ends.
There would be four in a range of $720^\circ$, because each period contributes two. This range is one period.

Both of them are vertical, so each has an equation of the form x = a number.
parts.workedSolution:
$\tan x$ has no value where the cosine underneath it is zero, and that happens at $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$ in this range.
So the asymptotes are the vertical lines $x = 90$ and $x = 270$.

commonErrors.feedback: $180^\circ$ is where the tangent curve crosses the axis, not where it breaks. The breaks are a quarter of a turn either side of it.

hints: Measure from one branch to the identical branch beside it.
parts.workedSolution: Every branch of the tangent curve is a copy of the one before it, and the branches sit $180^\circ$ apart, so the period is $180^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: $360^\circ$ is the period of sine and cosine. The tangent curve has already repeated itself once by then.

parts.stem:
Write down the value of $x$, strictly between $-180^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, at which your sketch crosses the x-axis and is also a point of the curve $y = \sin x$.

Answer ________ °

scheme.for: recognising that both curves pass through the origin

hints: $\tan x$ is zero at $-180^\circ$, $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.
$\sin x$ is also zero at all three, so look for the one that is a point of both curves and lies strictly between the ends of the range.
parts.workedSolution:
$\tan x = 0$ at $-180^\circ$, $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, and $\sin x$ is zero at each of them too.
The range is open at its ends here, so the value strictly inside it is $x = 0$.

commonErrors.feedback: $90^\circ$ is an asymptote of the tangent curve, so there is no point of the curve there at all.

questions.solutionProgram: tan zeros on [-180, 180]: -180, 0, 180; asymptotes at -90, 90; period 180

findTheMistake.stem: Órlaith is told that $\sin 50^\circ = 0.77$ and asked for the value of $\sin 130^\circ$. Her working:
studentWorking: 130 is past the maximum, so the curve is on its way down
180 - 50 = 130, so the two angles are a pair
Going down means the value is negative
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Lines 1 and 2 are exactly right: $130^\circ$ does sit on the falling part of the arch, and it is the mirror image of $50^\circ$ in the line $x = 90^\circ$.
Line 3 confuses falling with negative. Between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ the whole arch sits above the axis, so every value there is positive however steeply the curve is dropping.
The curve only goes below the axis after $180^\circ$, and $130^\circ$ is comfortably short of that.
correction: The mirror line x = 90 leaves the height unchanged
findTheMistake.feedback: The method mark is safe: spotting the pair is the part that is worth thinking about, and Órlaith spotted it. Sketch the arch and mark both angles on it before writing the value down, and the sign settles itself.

prompts.prompt: Give the five key points of $y = \sin x$ between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.
Give the five key points of $y = \cos x$ between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.
What is the period of each of the three curves?
prompts.answer: Sine and cosine repeat every 360 degrees; tangent repeats every 180 degrees.

prompts.prompt: Where are the asymptotes of $y = \tan x$, and what does the curve do at one?
prompts.answer: At 90 and 270 degrees, and at every angle 180 degrees from those. The curve gets closer and closer to the line without ever touching it.

prompts.prompt: A sketch has every key point plotted correctly. What else does the mark scheme want?
prompts.answer: One smooth curve with no straight sides, and a scale written on both axes.

prompts.prompt: How do you find a second solution of $\sin x = k$ once your calculator has given you the first?
prompts.answer: Take the first angle away from 180 degrees, or read the second crossing off the sketch: the arch is symmetrical about 90 degrees.

prompts.prompt: Why is $\cos(360^\circ - x) = \cos x$ rather than $\cos(180^\circ - x) = \cos x$?
prompts.answer: Because the cosine curve is symmetrical about 180 degrees, so 0 pairs with 360. The 180 minus rule belongs to sine, whose mirror is at 90 degrees.
